quarterly_data.signal: Q1 FY2026 results (CFO): revenue of $475 million, 14% of full-year guidance and in line with expectations. Adjusted gross profit was $27 million, an adjusted gross margin of 5.6%, well below the full-year expectation of 11% to 13%, because of approximately $20 million of additional cost, mostly on two specific projects outside the U.S. (scope changes, one in equipment and one in schedule, which management plans to recover under the contracts from customers over the rest of the year), plus the usual first-quarter pattern of lighter revenue against evenly spread fixed overhead. Adjusted EBITDA was negative $52 million. Rolling twelve-month adjusted gross margin is 12.3%. Total liquidity was approximately $1.1 billion: $477 million of ending cash plus $617 million available under credit facilities. The CFO said this liquidity is sufficient for the current plan, but the significant opportunities discussed on the call would require additional capital once they materialize, to be raised opportunistically.
quarterly_data.figure: revenue $475 million (14% of full-year guidance); adjusted gross margin 5.6%; adjusted EBITDA negative $52 million; approximately $20 million of additional cost; total liquidity approximately $1.1 billion

quarterly_data.signal: Record backlog of $5.5 billion, reflecting a clear step-up in U.S. contracting activity driven by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and rising demand forecasts; the midpoint of the FY2026 revenue outlook is now fully covered by backlog. Q1 orders were over $750 million globally; more than $500 million of them were in the U.S., which represented strong growth from prior quarters, with U.S. momentum building since the legislation passed last July. Management expects order growth across all core markets this year, with the U.S. about half of the total, and said Q1 order intake will be the low point of the year, with better intake to build visibility for '27. None of the new data-center targets has been converted into backlog yet.
quarterly_data.figure: record backlog $5.5 billion; Q1 orders over $750 million (more than $500 million in the U.S.)

quarterly_data.signal: FY2026 guidance REAFFIRMED at this call (point-in-time; the ranges introduced last quarter): revenue $3.2 to $3.6 billion with a midpoint of $3.4 billion; annual recurring revenue approximately $180 million by the end of fiscal 2026; adjusted EBITDA $40 million to $60 million; margins in the 11 to 13% range. The basis given: backlog covers the revenue midpoint, all equipment required to meet commitments has been ordered (minimizing supply-chain and commodity-price risk), and the operating cost structure is visible. The CEO said the company is committed to meeting the FY2026 guide rather than exceeding it and is working to make '27 the year it delivers good news. Longer-term framework: assume gross margins stay the same and EBITDA grows through operating leverage, with overhead growing at no more than half the rate of top-line growth. In Q&A the CFO described the blended margin guidance as 10 to 15%, depending on project scope (for example, with or without EPC).
quarterly_data.figure: revenue $3.2 to $3.6 billion (midpoint $3.4 billion); adjusted EBITDA $40 million to $60 million; ARR approximately $180 million; margins 11 to 13%

quarterly_data.signal: Pipeline grew by approximately $7 billion, or 30%, in the quarter, with the majority of the growth coming from the U.S., after sales efforts were ramped up in all core markets (expanded sales channels and outreach to existing and new customers). Demand is coming from developers, IPPs, utilities and rapidly expanding data-center opportunities. A project enters the pipeline only if management believes there is more than a 50% probability of it occurring within the next two years, because pipeline entries drive engineering, planning and cost decisions. Long-duration energy storage: early discussions on 34 gigawatt hours of projects, largely in Europe and the U.S., which management calls an additional growth opportunity since long-duration projects need more volume. Management clarified that the 60 figure given last quarter was a total addressable market, while the 34 gigawatt hours are actual projects in the pipeline or in leads.
quarterly_data.figure: pipeline up approximately $7 billion or 30%; long-duration projects 34 gigawatt hours

quarterly_data.signal: DATA CENTERS are the biggest new customer-segment opportunity. Fluence is in discussions covering 36 gigawatt hours of data-center projects, including customers with large portfolios such as hyperscalers, and is working through technical reviews with them. These are behind-the-meter or dedicated-line projects serving data centers directly; earlier front-of-the-meter work with renewable companies is not counted. Roughly 25% of the 36 gigawatt hours is in the pipeline today; many of the projects are not yet included, which management calls meaningful upside. None has been converted into backlog. Management expects "something happening" in the second half of the year (it cited the third or fourth quarter) but would not give a number, citing a new segment and competitive sensitivity. The CEO said the segment is growing very fast and that Fluence believes it has a competitive advantage over other technologies.
quarterly_data.figure: 36 gigawatt hours of data-center projects in discussion; roughly 25% in pipeline; none converted to backlog

quarterly_data.signal: Management listed four new and developing uses of battery storage by large energy users such as data centers and C&I facilities. (1) Speed to power: storage speeds grid interconnection by matching power demand to grid capability and avoids the delays and expense of grid upgrades. (2) Quality of power: injecting reactive power to resolve voltage disturbances, managing demand (including disconnecting from the grid when needed) and smooth ramp-rate control. (3) Backup power: replacing higher-cost, carbon-intensive thermal gensets. (4) Support of on-site, bring-your-own generation behind the meter. Quality of power needs a response time below ten milliseconds; Fluence has a road map to deliver it, and this is where it competes with other technologies. Current data-center demand comes more from speed-to-power and bring-your-own-generation applications than from quality of power. Management cited product density, safety, reliability and cybersecurity as advantages, and noted that Fluence does not compete with its data-center customers.
quarterly_data.figure: response time below ten milliseconds (quality-of-power requirement)

quarterly_data.signal: U.S. DOMESTIC SUPPLY CHAIN: the domestic-content supply chain now performs at the level the delivery schedule needs. Cell and module production is running ahead of plan, the enclosure manufacturing facility in Arizona is now on track, and the domestic supplier base is being expanded and diversified. On battery cells, Fluence is working with ASC (named AESC in the analyst's question) to resolve the prohibited foreign entity (PFE) status of ASC's Tennessee facility. Fluence made ASC an ownership proposal, but ASC gave assurances that it will meet the law's conditions another way, without Fluence joining the ownership structure; Fluence's priority is competitively priced, PFE-compliant cells. The 2026 delivery plan uses a roughly half-and-half mix of domestic and imported cells. Several U.S. facilities are converting EV battery lines to storage production; management compares this to China two or three years ago and sees it diversifying the supplier base toward multiple domestic cell partners. Management sees no real change in the competitive environment, only a significant diversification of battery-cell suppliers. It sees no need for vertical integration: contract manufacturers build Fluence's designs, and its system can integrate three or four different battery manufacturers.
quarterly_data.figure: domestic vs imported cell mix roughly half and half (2026 delivery plan)

quarterly_data.signal: Two pending legal matters were resolved. Moss Landing was settled for an immaterial amount, together with insurers and subcontractors on confidential terms, with a full release of claims and no admission of responsibility or liability for the 2021 overheating. On the Diablo Canyon project, Fluence obtained a court dismissal of Diablo's $230 million disgorgement claim.
